# Introduction

In this assignment we build two families of models on auto insurance
customer data: (1) binary logistic regression models predicting
`TARGET_FLAG`, whether a customer will crash their car, and (2) multiple
linear regression models predicting `TARGET_AMT`, the cost of the crash
given that one occurs.

# Data Exploration

```{r load-data}
#| label: load-data

train = read_csv("data/insurance-training-data.csv")
evaluation = read_csv("data/insurance-evaluation-data.csv")

train = train |> dplyr::select(-INDEX)
evaluation = evaluation |> dplyr::select(-INDEX)
```

## Size and Structure

The training dataset contains 8161 observations, 23 predictors, and 2
target variables. Of the 23 predictors, 13 are numeric and 10 are
categorical. Variables such as `INCOME` and `BLUEBOOK` are currently
coded as characters due to leading \$. These are transformed to numeric
variables for use in the models.

```{r data-structure}
#| label: data-structure

tibble(
  Variable = names(train),
  Type     = map_chr(train, ~ class(.x)[1]),
  Example  = map_chr(train, ~ paste(head(.x, 3), collapse = ", "))) |>
  kable()

dim(train)
```

```{r clean-fields}
#| label: clean-fields

train = train |>
  mutate(across(c(INCOME, HOME_VAL, BLUEBOOK, OLDCLAIM), 
                ~ as.numeric(str_replace_all(.x, "[^0-9.]", ""))),
         across(!where(is.numeric), as.factor))

evaluation = evaluation |>
  mutate(across(c(INCOME, HOME_VAL, BLUEBOOK, OLDCLAIM), 
                ~ as.numeric(str_replace_all(.x, "[^0-9.]", ""))),
         across(!where(is.numeric), as.factor))
```

## Summary Statistics

The table below shows summary statistics for all numeric predictors and
the two target variables in the training dataset. These give a quick
sense of what a typical value looks like for each variable, and how
widely the values spread. Some variables, such as `TARGET_AMT` and
`OLDCLAIM`, have a mean that is noticeably larger than the median (for
example, \$1504.32 vs. \$0.00). This suggests they are right-skewed. We
also see that variables are on very different scales, from small counts
like `CLM_FREQ` to dollar amounts like `HOME_VAL` that reach into the
hundreds of thousands. Because of the skew and scale differences, some
transformations and scaling will likely help the models fit better. We
discuss these in the Data Preparation section.

```{r summary-stats}
#| label: summary-stats

train |>
  dplyr::select(where(is.numeric)) |>
  describe() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("Variable") |>
  dplyr::select(Variable, mean, sd, median, se) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

## Distributions

The density and box plots below show the distributions of all the
numeric predictors. The two target variables are left out here and are
discussed separately. The plots show that the predictors have quite
different shapes. Some, like `AGE`, are roughly symmetric, while others,
like `BLUEBOOK`, are right-skewed. A few variables also have a large
spike at zero. Because many models work best when predictors are fairly
symmetric, transformations may help improve the fit.

```{r distributions}
#| label: fig-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of numeric variables"

train_long_num = pivot_longer(train, cols = where(is.numeric),
                              names_to = "variable", values_to = "value")

train_long_num |>
  filter(!variable %in% c("TARGET_AMT", "TARGET_FLAG")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_density(bins = 20, fill = "#3a86d4", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count", title = "Variable Distributions") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9.6)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-boxplots
#| fig-cap: "Boxplots of predictor and target variables"

train_long_num |>
  filter(!variable %in% c("TARGET_AMT", "TARGET_FLAG")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#3a86d4", colour = "black",
               outlier.colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Variable Distributions") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9.6) +
  coord_flip()
```

## Categorical Variables

The bar charts below show the distributions of the categorical
predictors, which gives a general idea of what categories are most and
least common, as well as how many categories each predictor has. Most
predictors, such as `PARENT1` and `REVOKED`, have an uneven distribution
that's dominated by one or a few categories. Other predictors, such as
`SEX`, are more evenly split. Categories with few customers may be hard
for a model to learn from, so we may need to combine some of them later.

```{r categorical}
#| label: fig-categorical
#| fig-cap: "Bar charts of categorical variables"

train_long_chr = pivot_longer(train, cols = !where(is.numeric),
                              names_to = "variable", values_to = "value")

train_long_chr |>
  count(variable, value, name = "count") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder_within(value, count, variable), y = count)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3a86d4", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_reordered() +
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 4,

  coord_flip() +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", ncol = 4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count", title = "Variable Distributions") +
```

## TARGET_FLAG Distribution

The table below shows the distribution of the target variable
`TARGET_FLAG`, where 1 means the customer was in a crash and 0 means
they were not. Roughly three out of four customers (73.62%) did not have
a crash, while about one in four (26.38%) did. This imbalance matters
for modeling because a model that simply predicted “no crash” for
everyone would be right about 74% of the time, so accuracy alone can be
misleading. We will need to look at other measures, such as sensitivity
and precision, when judging how well the models identify crashes.

```{r target-flag-dist}
#| label: target-flag-dist

train |>
  group_by(TARGET_FLAG) |>
  summarize(n = n()) |>
  mutate(pct = round(n/sum(n)*100, 2)) |>
  kable()
```

## TARGET_AMT Distribution

The density plot below shows the distribution of the target variable
`TARGET_AMT`, which is the cost of a crash. Customers who did not crash
have a cost of \$0, so those observations are removed from this plot,
since our goal is to predict the cost for customers who were in an
accident. The distribution is highly right-skewed, with most crashes
cost less than \$10,000, while a small number are very expensive.
Because those few large values can have a strong influence on a model, a
transformation such as a log transform may help. This is discussed
further in the Data Preparation section.

```{r target-amt-dist}
#| label: target-amt-dist

train |>
  filter(TARGET_AMT >0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = TARGET_AMT)) +
  geom_density(bins = 20, fill = "#3a86d4", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count", title = "TARGET_AMT Distribution") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9.6)
```

## Correlation with Targets

The figure below shows the correlations between all numeric predictors
and the two target variables. This helps us see whether any predictors
overlap with each other (collinearity), and which predictors may be
useful for predicting `TARGET_FLAG` and `TARGET_AMT`. The strongest
correlations between predictors are `INCOME` and `HOME_VAL`, followed by
`OLDCLAIM` and `CLM_FREQ`. This makes sense, since higher earners tend
to own more expensive homes, and customers with more claims tend to have
larger total claim amounts. The strongest correlations between a
predictor and a target are between `TARGET_FLAG` and both `MVR_PTS` and
`CLM_FREQ`, each at 0.22. This is fairly weak, which suggests that no
single predictor will explain much on its own, and the models will need
to combine several predictors. Finally, the two target variables have a
correlation of 0.53, which is expected because `TARGET_AMT` is always
\$0 when `TARGET_FLAG` is 0.

```{r correlation}
#| label: fig-correlation
#| fig-cap: "Correlation matrix of numeric variables"

cor_matrix <- train |>
  dplyr::select(where(is.numeric)) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

# Then we can plot the corr plot
corrplot(cor_matrix, method = "color", type = "lower", order = "hclust",
         addCoef.col = "black", number.cex = 0.6, tl.col = "black",
         tl.cex = 0.6, tl.srt = 45, diag = FALSE)
```

## Missing Data

The bar plot below shows the percentage of missing values for all
predictors and the two target variables. Six predictors have missing
values: `AGE`, `YOJ`, `INCOME`, `HOME_VAL`, `JOB`, and `CAR_AGE`. `JOB`
and `CAR_AGE` have the most, at just over 6% each. Because the missing
values are spread across different variables, removing every row with a
missing value would discard many customers, so these values will be
imputed instead. This is discussed further in the Data Preparation
section. Neither target variable has missing values, so no observations
need to be removed.

```{r missing-data}
#| label: missing-data

missing_props = train_long_num |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(proportion_missing = mean(is.na(value)), .groups = "drop") |>
  rbind(train_long_chr |>
          group_by(variable) |>
          summarise(proportion_missing = mean(is.na(value)), .groups = "drop"))

ggplot(missing_props, aes(x = reorder(variable, proportion_missing),
                          y = proportion_missing)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3a86d4") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Proportion missing", title = "Missing Data by Variable") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

# Data Preparation

Variables representing currency were cleaned (removing \$ and ,) prior
to generating the distributions. The remainder of the data preparation
is discussed in the following sections.

## Missing Value Imputation

As previously described, missing values are handled with imputation. We
used the `missRanger` R package, which fills in each missing value using
random forests, a flexible model that predicts the missing value from
the other columns. Instead of a simple fill-in such as the mean, median,
or mode, this uses information from the other predictors. For example, a
missing `HOME_VAL` can be estimated from a customer’s `INCOME` and
`JOB`, rather than from the overall average. The same imputation models
fit on the training data were then applied to the evaluation set, so
both datasets are treated in the same way. The table below confirms that
there are no missing values after imputation.

```{r impute}
#| label: impute

# Generate imputation method
imputation_fit = missRanger(as.data.frame(
  train |> dplyr::select(-TARGET_FLAG, -TARGET_AMT)), keep_forests = TRUE)

# Use imputation method on training dataset
train_imputed = imputation_fit$data |>
  mutate(TARGET_FLAG = train$TARGET_FLAG,
         TARGET_AMT = train$TARGET_AMT)

# Verify there are no more missing values
train_imputed |> summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.))))

# Apply imputation method on evaluation dataset
eval_imputed = predict(imputation_fit, newdata = evaluation |> 
                         dplyr::select(-TARGET_FLAG, -TARGET_AMT)) |>
  mutate(TARGET_FLAG = evaluation$TARGET_FLAG,
         TARGET_AMT = evaluation$TARGET_AMT)
```

## Feature Transformations

As noted earlier, several predictors are skewed rather than bell-shaped.
Transforming them to be more symmetric helps keep extreme values from
having too strong of an influence and generally leads to more stable
models. We used the Box-Cox transformation, a common method for reducing
skew. It requires all values to be strictly positive, so predictors
containing zero or negative values were first shifted so that their
minimum is 1. Shifting by a constant does not change the order or
relative spacing of the values. The table below shows the amount each
predictor was shifted by. The Box-Cox transformation was then applied to
the predictors that needed it.

```{r transformations}
#| label: transformations

num_data <- train_imputed |>
  dplyr::select(where(is.numeric), -TARGET_FLAG, -TARGET_AMT)

# Shift data that has values at or below 0.
shift_amt <- sapply(num_data, \(x) {
  m <- min(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (m <= 0) 1 - m else 0
})

# View which columns will get shifted.
shift_amt[shift_amt > 0] |>
  t() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  `rownames<-`("") |>
  kable()

# Function that adds the stored shift to each column.
apply_shift <- function(df, shifts) {
  for (col in names(shifts)) df[[col]] <- df[[col]] + shifts[[col]]
  df
}

# Apply the shift, then apply Box-Cox, center, and scale.
num_shifted <- apply_shift(num_data, shift_amt)
```

The table below shows the lambda values used for each predictor. Lambda
is the power the data is raised to, with a value of 0 corresponding to a
log transformation. After transformation, the numeric predictors were
also centered and scaled so that each has a mean of 0 and a standard
deviation of 1. Because the predictors are measured on very different
scales (for example, `CLM_FREQ` versus `HOME_VAL`), this puts them on
equal footing, makes the coefficients easier to compare, and helps the
model fit more reliably.

```{r pre-process}
#| label: pre-process

pp <- preProcess(num_shifted, method = c("BoxCox", "center", "scale"))
lambdas <- sapply(pp$bc, \(x) x$lambda)
lambdas

train_pp <- predict(pp, num_shifted)
train_pp = train_pp |> cbind(train_imputed |>
                               dplyr::select(!where(is.numeric), TARGET_FLAG, TARGET_AMT))

# Apply same shift and pre-processing to evaluation data.
eval_shifted <- apply_shift(eval_imputed |> dplyr::select(all_of(names(num_data))), shift_amt)
eval_pp <- predict(pp, as.data.frame(eval_shifted))
eval_pp = eval_pp |> cbind(eval_imputed |>
                             dplyr::select(!where(is.numeric), TARGET_FLAG, TARGET_AMT))
```

The output below shows the recommended Box-Cox lambda for the target
variable `TARGET_AMT`. This was calculated using only customers who were
in an accident, since the \$0 values for all other customers will not be
part of the model. The recommended lambda value is 0, which points to a
log transformation. The density plot below shows `TARGET_AMT` after the
log transformation, which is much more symmetric than before, such that
the log transformation will be used in the models.

```{r target-amt-process}
#| label: target-amt-process

train_pp |>
  filter(TARGET_AMT > 0) |>
  dplyr::select(TARGET_AMT) |>
  preProcess(method = c("BoxCox"))

train_pp_linear = train_pp |>
  filter(TARGET_AMT > 0)

train_pp |>
  pivot_longer(cols = where(is.numeric), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!variable %in% c("TARGET_FLAG", "TARGET_AMT")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_density(bins = 20, fill = "#3a86d4", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count", title = "Variable Distributions") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9.6)
```

## Training Set Splitting for Logistic Model

When developing a model, it is good practice to split the full training
data into two parts: a training set and a test set. The model is built
using the training set and then used to predict outcomes for the test
set. Checking performance on the test set matters because a model will
always look best on the data it was built from. The test set shows how
the model is likely to perform on new customers. We split the data 80/20
at random, but did so in a stratified way, meaning the proportion of
customers with and without a crash (`TARGET_FLAG`) is kept the same in
both sets. This is important because crashes are the minority outcome,
and an unlucky random split could leave one set with noticeably fewer of
them. In the full training data, about 73.6% of customers did not crash.
The two tables below show that both the training set and the test set
also have about 73.6% of customers without a crash.

```{r split-train-log}
#| label: split-train-log

set.seed(313)
train_partition = createDataPartition(train_pp$TARGET_FLAG, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train_log_part = train_pp[train_partition, ]
test_log_part = train_pp[-train_partition, ]

train_log_part |>
  group_by(TARGET_FLAG) |>
  summarize(n = n()) |>
  mutate(pct = round(n/sum(n)*100, 2)) |>
  kable()

test_log_part |>
  group_by(TARGET_FLAG) |>
  summarize(n = n()) |>
  mutate(pct = round(n/sum(n)*100, 2)) |>
  kable()
```

## Training Set Splitting for Linear Model

As with the logistic model, the data is divided into a training set and
a test set for the linear model. Because the linear model predicts the
cost of a crash, we first filtered the full training data to only the
customers who were in a crash, and then split those customers 80/20.
Unlike the logistic split, this one is not stratified. The outcome here
is a dollar amount rather than a yes/no category, so there are no group
proportions to preserve, and a random split should give two sets with
similar costs.

```{r split-train-linear}
#| label: split-train-linear

set.seed(313)
train_partition_line = createDataPartition(train_pp_linear$TARGET_AMT, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train_line_part = train_pp_linear[train_partition_line, ]
test_line_part = train_pp_linear[-train_partition_line, ]
```

# Build Models

## Logistic Regression Models (`TARGET_FLAG`)

For the purposes of this report, three separate logistic models are
generated. The performance of the three models will be compared and used
to select a model for predicting on the evaluation dataset.

### Logistic Model 1

The first logistic model uses all of the predictors. The summary below
shows the results. Each categorical predictor is split into dummy
variables, with one category left out to serve as the reference group.
The coefficients for the other categories are interpreted relative to
that reference. For example, for `SEX`, Male is the reference, so only a
Female coefficient appears. Of the 13 numeric predictors, 10 are
statistically significant (p \< 0.05). Of the 10 categorical predictors,
5 are significant for every category shown, three are not significant
for any category, and two (`EDUCATION` and `JOB`) are significant for
only some of their categories. The model has an Akaike Information
Criterion (AIC) of 5870.9. AIC balances how well the model fits against
how many predictors it uses, with lower values being better, and it will
be used to compare models along with accuracy, sensitivity, and
specificity.

```{r logit-1}
#| label: logit-1

log_train_data = train_log_part |> dplyr::select(-TARGET_AMT)
log_test_data = test_log_part |> dplyr::select(-TARGET_AMT)

log_train_model1 = glm(TARGET_FLAG ~ ., family = binomial, log_train_data)
summary(log_train_model1)
```

### Logistic Model 2

The second logistic model uses a subset of the predictors: `AGE`,
`CAR_AGE`, `CAR_USE`, `CLM_FREQ`, `INCOME`, `JOB`, `KIDSDRIV`,
`MVR_PTS`, `OLDCLAIM`, `REVOKED`, and `TRAVTIME`. These include
predictors that had the strongest correlations with `TARGET_FLAG`, such
as `MVR_PTS` and `CLM_FREQ`, as well as others that logically relate to
crash risk. For example, `KIDSDRIV` is included because teenagers in the
household are often new drivers, and new drivers tend to crash more
often.

The summary below shows the results of the second model. Of the 8
numeric predictors, 7 are statistically significant (p \< 0.05). Of the
3 categorical predictors, 2 are significant for every category shown,
while `JOB` is significant for only some of its categories. The model
has an AIC of 6635.8, about 765 higher than the first logistic model,
which suggests it fits worse. However, a simpler model can still be the
better choice, so this is explored further in the Select Models section.

```{r logit-2}
#| label: logit-2

# Subset of predictors selected
log_train_data2 = log_train_data |>
  dplyr::select(AGE, CAR_AGE, CAR_USE, CLM_FREQ, INCOME, JOB, KIDSDRIV, MVR_PTS, OLDCLAIM,
                REVOKED, TRAVTIME, TARGET_FLAG)
log_test_data2 = log_test_data |>
  dplyr::select(AGE, CAR_AGE, CAR_USE, CLM_FREQ, INCOME, JOB, KIDSDRIV, MVR_PTS, OLDCLAIM,
                REVOKED, TRAVTIME, TARGET_FLAG)

log_train_model2 = glm(TARGET_FLAG ~ ., family = binomial, log_train_data2)
summary(log_train_model2)
```

### Logistic Model 3

The third logistic model uses backward step-wise elimination to choose
its predictors. The process starts with all of the predictors, as in the
first logistic model. At each step, the predictor whose removal improves
the model’s AIC the most is dropped, and the model is refit with the
smaller set of predictors. This repeats until removing any more
predictors no longer improves the AIC. The result is a simpler model
that keeps only the predictors that provide meaningful contributions.

The summary below shows the results of the third model. After
elimination, 10 of the original 13 numeric predictors and 7 of the
original 10 categorical predictors remain. All of the retained numeric
predictors are statistically significant (p \< 0.05), and each retained
categorical predictor has at least one significant category. The model
has an AIC of 5861.4, which is 9.5 lower than the first logistic model.
This suggests a slightly better fit with fewer predictors. This is
explored further in the Select Models section using other metrics, such
as accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity.

```{r logit-3}
#| label: logit-3

log_train_model3 = step(log_train_model1, direction = "backward", trace = 1)
summary(log_train_model3)
```

## Linear Regression Models (`TARGET_AMT`)

As previously stated, the linear models are fitted on the training
dataset that was filtered to only include customers who were in a crash.
This is to remove any potential bias from observations where the
customer was not in a crash (and thus had a cost of \$0).

### Linear Model 1

As with the first logistic model, the first linear model, which predicts
`TARGET_AMT`, uses all of the predictors. It is fit only on customers
who were in a crash, and it predicts the log of `TARGET_AMT`, since the
earlier Box-Cox analysis recommended a log transformation to make the
costs more symmetric. As a result, predictions from this model are
exponentiated to convert them back to dollars.

The summary below shows the results. Of the 13 numeric predictors, only
one is statistically significant (p \< 0.05): `BLUEBOOK`, which
represents the value of the vehicle. Its coefficient is positive,
meaning that the cost increases as the value of the vehicle increases.
This logically makes sense, as it is typically more expensive to fix a
more valuable vehicle. None of the 10 categorical predictors are
statistically significant. The model has an RSE of 0.8149 (on the log
scale) and an R² of about 0.029, meaning it explains only about 3% of
the variation in crash costs. This suggests a poor fit, which is
explored further in the Select Models section.

```{r lm-1}
#| label: lm-1

linear_train_data = train_line_part |> dplyr::select(-TARGET_FLAG)
linear_test_data = test_line_part |> dplyr::select(-TARGET_FLAG)

linear_train_model1 = lm(log(TARGET_AMT) ~ ., data = linear_train_data)
summary(linear_train_model1)
```

### Linear Model 2

The second linear model uses backward stepwise elimination to choose its
predictors, as in the third logistic model. Only four of the original 23
predictors were kept: `BLUEBOOK`, `MVR_PTS`, `MSTATUS`, and `SEX`. The
summary below shows the results. The model has an RSE of 0.8115 (on the
log scale) and an R² of about 0.019, meaning it explains only about 2%
of the variation in crash costs. The R² is slightly lower than the first
linear model’s (0.029), which is expected when predictors are removed,
while the RSE is slightly better. In other words, the second model
performs about as well as the first while being much simpler. Both
models explain very little of the variation in cost, which is explored
further in the Select Models section.

```{r lm-2}
#| label: lm-2

linear_train_model2 = step(linear_train_model1, direction = "backward", trace = 1)
summary(linear_train_model2)
```

## Coefficient Discussion

For the purposes of discussing the coefficients of the models, only
predictors that were statistically significant (p \< 0.05) are
discussed.

Across all three logistic models, most coefficients have a direction
that makes sense. For example, `REVOKED` and `KIDSDRIV` are positive in
every model, which fits the idea that customers with a revoked license
or teenage drivers in the household are higher-risk.

Two predictors are less intuitive. In the first model, `HOMEKIDS` has a
positive coefficient, meaning more children at home goes with a higher
chance of a crash. One might expect parents to drive more cautiously,
though the model may be picking up the effects of related predictors. In
the second and third models, `OLDCLAIM` is negative, even though higher
past claim totals would be expected to mean higher crash risk. A likely
reason is that `OLDCLAIM` overlaps with `CLM_FREQ`. Once the model
accounts for the number of past claims, a higher dollar total may simply
reflect a few expensive claims rather than a riskier driver.

In both linear models, `BLUEBOOK` is statistically significant (p \<
0.05) and has a positive coefficient, which makes sense, since a more
expensive vehicle costs more to repair or replace. The second linear
model also finds `MVR_PTS`, the number of points on the driver’s record,
to be significant and positive. This is plausible, since drivers with
more violations may be higher-risk and possibly involved in more severe
crashes, though this link is less direct than the one for `BLUEBOOK`.
All significant coefficients have a sensible direction, but because both
models explain only a small share of the variation in crash cost, these
effects are minimal.

# Select Models

## Multicollinearity

The table below shows the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) for the
predictors in each of the three logistic models. VIF measures how much a
predictor overlaps with the other predictors, which is known as
multicollinearity. When predictors overlap heavily, the model has
trouble separating their individual effects. A VIF above 5 is a common
warning sign. In all three logistic models, `OLDCLAIM` and `CLM_FREQ`
both have a VIF above 19, indicating a high level of multicollinearity,
while the remaining predictors are below the benchmark. This is
consistent with the earlier explanation for the surprising negative sign
of `OLDCLAIM`. Because the two predictors carry much of the same
information, it may be beneficial to remove one of them, in a future
model.

```{r vif}
#| label: vif

get_vif_adj <- function(model) {
  v <- vif(model)
  if (is.matrix(v)) {
    tibble(Term = rownames(v),
           VIF_adj = v[, "GVIF^(1/(2*Df))"]^2)
  } else {
    tibble(Term = names(v), VIF_adj = as.numeric(v))
  }
}

list(
  "Model 1: All Features"       = log_train_model1,
  "Model 2: Pruned"             = log_train_model2,
  "Model 3: Backward Elimination" = log_train_model3
) |>
  map(get_vif_adj) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "Model") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Model, values_from = VIF_adj) |>
  arrange(desc(`Model 1: All Features`)) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Adjusted VIF by Model")
```

The table below shows the VIF for the predictors in the two linear
models. Similar to the logistic models, the only sign of
multicollinearity is between `OLDCLAIM` and `CLM_FREQ` in the first
model with all predictors, suggesting that one of these should be
removed from the model. However, neither of these are included in the
second linear model that utilized backward step-wise elimination to
select the predictors.

```{r line-vif}
#| label: line-vif

list(
  "Model 1: All Features"         = linear_train_model1,
  "Model 2: Backward Elimination" = linear_train_model2
) |>
  map(get_vif_adj) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "Model") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Model, values_from = VIF_adj) |>
  arrange(desc(`Model 1: All Features`)) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Adjusted VIF by Model")
```

## Logistic Model Evaluation

A confusion matrix is generated for each of the 3 logistic models, both
for the training set and test set. All 6 of the confusion matrices can
be found below.

```{r logit-eval}
#| label: logit-eval

get_metrics = function(model, data, model_name, set_name) {
  
  probs = predict(model, newdata = data, type = "response")
  pred_class = ifelse(probs > 0.5, 1, 0)

  cm = confusionMatrix(factor(pred_class, levels = c(0, 1)),
                        factor(data$TARGET_FLAG, levels = c(0, 1)),
                        positive = "1")

  auc_val = as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(data$TARGET_FLAG, probs, quiet = TRUE)))

  metrics = data.frame(
    Model       = model_name,
    Set         = set_name,
    Accuracy    = cm$overall[["Accuracy"]],
    Error_Rate  = 1 - cm$overall[["Accuracy"]],
    Precision   = cm$byClass[["Precision"]],
    Sensitivity = cm$byClass[["Sensitivity"]],
    Specificity = cm$byClass[["Specificity"]],
    F1          = cm$byClass[["F1"]],
    AUC         = auc_val
  )
  
  list(metrics = metrics, cm = cm$table)
}

m1_train <- get_metrics(log_train_model1, log_train_data, "Model 1", "Train")
m1_test  <- get_metrics(log_train_model1, log_test_data,  "Model 1", "Test")
m2_train <- get_metrics(log_train_model2, log_train_data, "Model 2", "Train")
m2_test  <- get_metrics(log_train_model2, log_test_data,  "Model 2", "Test")
m3_train <- get_metrics(log_train_model3, log_train_data, "Model 3", "Train")
m3_test  <- get_metrics(log_train_model3, log_test_data,  "Model 3", "Test")

kable(m1_train$cm, caption = "Model 1 - Train Set")
kable(m1_test$cm, caption = "Model 1 - Test")
kable(m2_train$cm, caption = "Model 2 - Train Set")
kable(m2_test$cm, caption = "Model 2 - Test Set")
kable(m3_train$cm, caption = "Model 3 - Train Set")
kable(m3_test$cm, caption = "Model 3 - Test Set")
```

The table below summarizes the performance metrics for the logistic
models on both the training and test sets. The benchmark for accuracy is
73.6%, the share of customers who were not in a crash, since a model
that predicted “no crash” for everyone would be right that often. On the
training set, models 1 and 3 had the same accuracy of 79.3%. On the test
set, model 3 performed best at 77.9%. Overall, the models beat the
benchmark by only about 4 to 6 percentage points, so none are
particularly strong at classifying customers correctly.

Sensitivity is the share of actual crashes a model correctly identifies,
and specificity is the share of non-crashes it correctly identifies. All
three models are much better at identifying non-crashes, with
specificity of 90.9% to 94.1% but sensitivity of only 24.4% to 43.9%. In
other words, the models miss most of the customers who actually crash,
which is expected given that only about one in four customers crashes
and a 0.5 cutoff is used. Model 2 has the best specificity on the test
set but the worst sensitivity, while Model 3 has the best sensitivity
and the second-best specificity. Model 3 also has the highest F1 score
on the test set, which balances how many predicted crashes are correct
against how many actual crashes are found. For AUC, which measures how
well a model ranks crashes above non-crashes, Model 3 is second, behind
Model 1 by only 0.002.

The second table below shows the AIC for each model. Model 3, which used
backward step-wise elimination, has the lowest, and Model 2 has the
highest. AIC is calculated on the training data, so it is a supporting
check rather than a test-set measure.

```{r logit-metrics}
#| label: logit-eval

results <- rbind(m1_train$metrics, m1_test$metrics,
                 m2_train$metrics, m2_test$metrics,
                 m3_train$metrics, m3_test$metrics)

kable(results, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)


data.frame(Model = c("Model 1", "Model 2", "Model 3"),
           AIC = c(AIC(log_train_model1), AIC(log_train_model2), AIC(log_train_model3))) |>
  kable(digits = 1, rownames = FALSE)
```

## Linear Model Evaluation

The table below shows the performance metrics for the two linear models
on both the training and test sets. The Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) is
the typical size of the prediction error, in dollars, so lower is
better. Both models perform slightly better on the test set than on the
training set, which is unexpected. This is most likely random variation,
since the test set is small and a few very expensive claims can shift
the results. The R² values are both close to 0, which shows that neither
model explains much of the variation in crash costs. Note that these R²
values differ from the ones in the model summaries, because the
summaries are on the log scale, while the values in the table are
calculated on dollar amounts after the predictions were exponentiated.
Finally, the F-statistic tests whether a model explains more variation
than a model with no predictors, such that a higher value provides more
evidence that it does. Looking at the F-statistics of the two linear
models, Model 2 has a higher value, which reflects that it achieves a
similar fit with fewer predictors.

```{r lm-eval}
#| label: lm-eval
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for the selected linear model"

get_lm_metrics <- function(model, data, model_name, set_name) {
  
  pred   <- exp(predict(model, newdata = data))
  actual <- data$TARGET_AMT
  
  sse <- sum((actual - pred)^2)
  sst <- sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)
  
  f_stat <- NA_real_
  if (set_name == "Train") {
    f_stat <- unname(summary(model)$fstatistic["value"])
  }
  
  data.frame(
    Model  = model_name,
    Set    = set_name,
    RMSE   = sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2)),
    R2     = 1 - sse / sst,   # R-squared in dollars
    F_stat = f_stat
  )
}

lm_results <- rbind(
  get_lm_metrics(linear_train_model1, linear_train_data, "Model 1", "Train"),
  get_lm_metrics(linear_train_model1, linear_test_data,  "Model 1", "Test"),
  get_lm_metrics(linear_train_model2, linear_train_data, "Model 2", "Train"),
  get_lm_metrics(linear_train_model2, linear_test_data,  "Model 2", "Test")
)

kable(lm_results, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The two sets of residual plots provide diagnostics for the linear models
predicting `TARGET_AMT`. The residuals-versus-fitted plots check whether
the models missed any pattern, the Q-Q plots check whether the errors
are roughly bell-shaped, and the leverage plots check for unusually
influential points. For both models, the residuals are centered around 0
with a fairly even spread, and the Q-Q plots follow the line closely
apart from the tails \[adjust to match your plots\]. No points appear to
have an outsized influence. Because the diagnostics and the performance
metrics are very similar for both models, Model 2 is selected since it
achieves the same results with fewer predictors. Note that these checks
only show that the model’s assumptions are reasonable. The low R² still
means both models explain little of the variation in crash cost.

```{r lm-residuals}
#| label: lm-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for the selected linear model"

plot(linear_train_model1)
plot(linear_train_model2)
```

## Final Model Selection

Based on the results in the previous sections, the third logistic model
and the second linear model are selected for predicting on the
evaluation set. Both were built using backward stepwise elimination,
which removes unnecessary predictors. The third logistic model had the
best sensitivity and F1 score on the test set, the lowest AIC, and an
AUC nearly tied with the first model, while using fewer predictors. The
second linear model performed about the same as the first, so it is
chosen for its simplicity.

# Predictions on Evaluation Data

The two selected models are used to predict on the evaluation set. The
evaluation set was preprocessed in the same way as the training data,
including imputation, transformations, centering, and scaling, using the
values calculated from the training data. The logistic model gives the
probability of a crash, which is classified using the 0.5 threshold. The
linear model predicts the log of `TARGET_AMT`, so its outputs are
exponentiated to convert them to dollars.

The table below shows the distribution of the predicted `TARGET_FLAG`
values. About 81.7% of customers (1750 out of 2141) are predicted not to
crash, compared with 73.6% in the training data, a difference of about 8
percentage points. This is expected, since the model has low sensitivity
at the 0.5 threshold and therefore predicts fewer crashes than actually
occur.

```{r predictions}
#| label: predictions

eval_log = predict(log_train_model3, newdata = eval_pp |> dplyr::select(-TARGET_AMT),
                   type = "response")

eval_pp_updated = eval_pp |>
  mutate(
    P_TARGET_FLAG = eval_log,
    TARGET_FLAG   = ifelse(eval_log > 0.5, 1, 0),
    pred_amt      = exp(predict(linear_train_model2, newdata = eval_pp)),
    TARGET_AMT    = ifelse(TARGET_FLAG == 1, pred_amt, 0)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(-pred_amt)

eval_pp_updated |>
  group_by(TARGET_FLAG) |>
  summarize(n = n()) |>
  mutate(pct = round(n/sum(n)*100, 2)) |>
  kable()
```

The density plot below shows the distribution of predicted `TARGET_AMT`
for the 391 customers predicted to be in a crash. The predictions range
from about \$3,000 to \$5,000, with a peak just under \$4,000. This is
much narrower than the actual crash costs in the training data, which
have a long tail of very expensive claims. There are two likely reasons.
First, the linear model explains very little of the variation in cost,
so it predicts similar amounts for most customers. Second,
exponentiating a log-scale prediction gives a typical (median) cost
rather than the average, and because a few very large claims pull the
average up, the predictions tend to run low.

```{r eval-target-amt}
#| label: eval-target-amt

eval_pp_updated |>
  filter(TARGET_FLAG == 1) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = TARGET_AMT)) +
  geom_density(bins = 20, fill = "#3a86d4", colour = "white") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 7500)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count", title = "TARGET_AMT Distribution") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9.6)
```

## Conclusion

The goal of this report was to build models that predict whether a
customer will be in a car crash (`TARGET_FLAG`) and, if they are, how
much the crash will cost (`TARGET_AMT`). The training data contains
8,161 customers, with about 26% of them being in a crash. Several
predictors were skewed, and six had missing values. These issues were
handled with random forest imputation, Box-Cox transformations, and
centering and scaling. The cost target was log transformed since the
Box-Cox method recommended it.

Three logistic models and two linear models were built and compared. The
third logistic model, which used backward step-wise elimination, was
selected to predict crashes. It had the lowest AIC, the best sensitivity
and F1 score on the test set, and an AUC nearly tied with the first
model, while using fewer predictors. Its accuracy of about 77.9% on the
test set beats the 73.6% benchmark for always predicting “no crash” by
only a few percentage points, and it misses most of the customers who
actually crash at the 0.5 threshold. The second linear model, also built
with backward step-wise elimination, was selected to predict cost. It
performed about the same as the first linear model, but with only four
predictors.

The biggest limitation is the cost model. Both linear models explain
only about 2% to 3% of the variation in crash costs, so the predicted
costs fall in a narrow range of about \$3,000 to \$5,000 and miss the
very expensive claims. This is partly because exponentiating log-scale
predictions gives a typical cost rather than an average. The available
predictors appear to say much more about whether a crash will happen
than about how costly it will be.
